query: How can melting temperature, enthalpy and entropy of fusion, volume change at melting, and liquid-phase thermodynamic properties be determined accurately and efficiently across the high-entropy-alloy family? State the physical rationale, expected quantitative performance, range of applicability, supporting prior evidence, and a decisive validation result that would rule out the proposed approach.

generation.hypothesis: A combined high-throughput calorimetry and CALPHAD-based computational approach can reliably determine melting temperature, enthalpy/entropy of fusion, volume change at melting, and liquid-phase thermodynamic properties for a broad spectrum of high-entropy alloys.
generation.material_initial_state: Polycrystalline high-entropy alloy samples prepared via standard arc-melting or powder metallurgy routes, homogenized to minimize compositional gradients.
generation.intervention: Apply systematic high-throughput differential scanning calorimetry (DSC) or drop-calorimetry measurements in tandem with CALPHAD-type computational modeling across the targeted composition space of high-entropy alloys.
generation.conditions: Measurements carried out over 300–1800 K temperature range in inert atmospheres; computational parameters validated against known phase equilibria and thermochemical reference data for simpler alloys.
generation.structural_mediator: Large configurational entropy from multiple principal elements; partial local ordering and variations in mixing enthalpy influence the melting behavior and thermodynamics.
generation.mechanism: Combining experimental calorimetry and validated thermodynamic models captures both the intrinsic multicomponent entropy contribution and the enthalpic interactions among constituent elements, enabling accurate property predictions across diverse compositions.
generation.predicted_outcome: Average uncertainties below ±10 K for melting temperature, ±5–10% for enthalpy of fusion, ±5–10% for entropy of fusion, and volumetric changes at melting within ±0.3% of reference dilatometry data.
generation.baseline: Typical uncertainties with single-method approaches can exceed ±30 K for melting temperatures and ±15–20% for enthalpy/entropy assessments of multi-component alloys.
generation.boundary: Most accurate for high-entropy alloys with five or more principal components and near-homogeneous solid solutions; improvements in both experimental calibration and computational databases are needed for alloys with significant short-range ordering or intermetallic phases.
generation.uncertainty: Correlations between computed and measured data might deviate for oversimplified or incomplete thermodynamic descriptions, especially in highly segregated or kinetically constrained systems.

falsification_experiment.design: Select a subset of high-entropy alloys covering a range of compositions and systematically measure melting temperature, heat of fusion, and volume change using high-temperature DSC, X-ray diffraction, and dilatometry. Compare to CALPHAD-derived predictions that include known baseline thermodynamic parameters. Cross-check with controlled doping experiments that selectively change one element’s concentration.
measurements: Differential scanning calorimetry to obtain precise melting profiles and enthalpies of fusion.
High-temperature X-ray diffraction or dilatometry to quantify volume change at melt onset.
Thermodynamic calculations (CALPHAD or related models) to predict the same properties for each composition.
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the experimentally measured values systematically deviate from the predicted properties by more than 30 K for melting temperature or 20% for enthalpy/entropy across multiple compositions, the hypothesis that a combined high-throughput calorimetry and CALPHAD model can accurately capture multi-component behavior is falsified.
